title: Spinal Cord
subtitle: Placing a myelopathy by sensory level, tract pattern, vascular territory and cord segment

points.text: The cervical enlargement (the arms) spans C5 to T1; the lumbar enlargement (the legs) spans L3 to S2.
points.quote: The cervical enlargement corresponds to the segmental innervation of the upper extremities and extends from C5 to T1 spinal levels

points.text: The adult conus medullaris ends at L1-L2, reached by about 2 months of age.
points.quote: By the age of 2 months, the conus has reached the adult L1-L2 level

points.text: Lumbar and sacral roots run down in the subarachnoid space and form the cauda equina around the filum terminale.
points.quote: This lower group of nerve roots congregates around the filum terminale in the spinal theca and is known as the cauda equina.

points.text: Spinous processes do not match cord segments in the thoracic region: two segments off in the upper thoracic region, three in the lower; T11 overlies L3 cord.
points.quote: in the lower thoracic region, there is a discrepancy of three segments. The eleventh thoracic spinous process overlies the third lumbar cord segment

points.text: Pain and temperature cross in the ventral white commissure and ascend in the contralateral lateral spinothalamic tract to the VPL thalamus.
points.quote: they then proceed to the ventrolateral quadrant of the spinal cord and ascend as the lateral spinothalamic (neospinothalamic) tract to reach the thalamus

points.text: Spinothalamic lamination: cervical fibers lie dorsomedially and sacral fibers ventrolaterally, which explains why an extramedullary lesion can give a sensory level far below it.
points.quote: fibers carrying information from cervical regions are situated dorsomedially, and those from sacral regions are situated ventrolaterally.

points.text: In the dorsal columns, the fasciculus gracilis carries the lower body medially and the fasciculus cuneatus the upper body laterally.
points.quote: the lowermost part of the body (sacral, lumbar, and the lowest six thoracic levels) are located more medially and constitute the fasciculus gracilis

points.text: Most corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla and descend as the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus.
points.quote: descend in a massive projection tract in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord known as the lateral corticospinal tract

points.text: The uncrossed remainder descends in the ipsilateral ventral funiculus as the ventral corticospinal tract.
points.quote: descend in the ipsilateral ventral funiculus as the ventral corticospinal tract

points.text: Ventral horn somatotopy: flexor motor neurons lie dorsal to extensor motor neurons.
points.quote: ventral horn neurons innervating flexor muscles lie dorsal to those neurons innervating extensor muscles.

points.text: Sulcal branches of the anterior spinal artery supply the anterior horn, lateral horn and central gray matter.
points.quote: Sulcal branches of the anterior spinal artery supply the anterior horn, the lateral horn, the central gray matter

points.text: The paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal horns and the dorsal funiculi (dorsal columns).
points.quote: The posterior spinal arteries also extend throughout the length of the spinal cord and supply the dorsal horns and the dorsal funiculi.

points.text: The midthoracic cord (T3-T8) is the poorly vascularized region.
points.quote: which is poorly vascularized, is supplied by branches of the intercostal arteries and includes the third through the eighth thoracic segments

points.text: The great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz (artery of the lumbar enlargement) most often enters from the left, usually with a T9-T12 root.
points.quote: the great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz (artery of the lumbar enlargement), which most frequently enters from the left side

localizationRules.rule: Look for the pin-prick sensory level
localizationRules.explanation: Pin-prick loss below a segmental level is the most useful localizing sign, but with extramedullary lesions the level can sit many segments below the lesion because of spinothalamic lamination.
localizationRules.quote: With extramedullary cord lesions, a sensory level may be found many segments below the level of the lesion.

localizationRules.rule: Segmental LMN signs at the lesion, UMN signs below
localizationRules.explanation: Ventral horn or root damage at the level of the lesion gives lower motor neuron signs in that myotome; the tracts below give upper motor neuron signs.
localizationRules.quote: At the level of the lesion, there are segmental lower motor neuron (LMN) signs (paresis, atrophy, fasciculations, and areflexia)

localizationRules.explanation: Paresthesias that progress downward suggest an intramedullary lesion; those that ascend suggest an extramedullary lesion.
localizationRules.quote: Descending progression of paresthesias suggests intramedullary lesions; conversely, ascending progression of paresthesias suggests extramedullary lesions.

localizationRules.explanation: Dissociated sensory loss, sacral sparing and vibration worse than position sense point to an intramedullary lesion.
localizationRules.quote: Dissociated sensory loss and sacral sparing and greater impairment of vibratory sense than position sense characterize intramedullary lesions.

localizationRules.explanation: Unilateral dermatomal pain worse with cough or Valsalva is more common with extradural than intramedullary lesions and can be the first sign.
localizationRules.quote: More common with extradural lesions and unusual with intramedullary lesions, radicular pain may occur in isolation before the development of dermatomal hypesthesia

keySyndromes.name: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection)
keySyndromes.triad: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature + ipsilateral loss of proprioception below the lesion + ipsilateral spastic weakness with hyperreflexia and Babinski sign (+ segmental LMN and sensory signs at the level)
keySyndromes.clue: Crossed spinothalamic loss on the opposite side, with dorsal column and corticospinal signs on the same side as the lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: Impaired pain and temperature sensation contralateral to the hemisection due to interruption of the crossed spinothalamic tract.

keySyndromes.name: Central cord syndrome (syringomyelia)
keySyndromes.triad: Bilateral suspended (vest-like) loss of pain and temperature + preserved soft touch and proprioception + segmental atrophy, paresis and areflexia at the level
keySyndromes.clue: Decussating spinothalamic fibers are hit first, so sensory loss is dissociated; later spread can add Horner syndrome, spastic paralysis below and dorsal column signs.
keySyndromes.quote: There is preservation of soft touch and proprioception (dissociation of sensory loss).

keySyndromes.name: Posterolateral column disease (subacute combined degeneration)
keySyndromes.triad: Loss of proprioception and vibration in the legs + sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign + spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski signs
keySyndromes.clue: Pain and temperature stay intact because the spinothalamic tracts are spared; ankle reflexes may be depressed from superimposed neuropathy.
keySyndromes.quote: include loss of proprioception and vibration sense in the legs, as well as sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign

keySyndromes.name: Tabes dorsalis (posterior column disease)
keySyndromes.clue: Lightning pains are a hallmark; limbs are hypotonic but not weak; patellar and ankle reflexes are absent.
keySyndromes.quote: Classic signs (triad of the 3As) include Argyll Robertson pupils, areflexia, and ataxia

keySyndromes.name: Anterior spinal artery infarct
keySyndromes.triad: Sudden back or neck pain + flaccid areflexic paraplegia + impaired pain and temperature to a sensory level + preserved proprioception and vibration + urinary incontinence
keySyndromes.clue: The posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns, so position, vibration and light touch are spared; the posterior spinal artery syndrome is the reverse.
keySyndromes.quote: Position, vibration, and light touch remain intact due to preservation of the dorsal columns, which are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries.

keySyndromes.name: Conus medullaris versus cauda equina
keySyndromes.triad: Conus: early sphincter dysfunction + late pain + symmetric saddle anesthesia; cauda equina: early radicular pain + asymmetric sensory loss + late sphincter changes
keySyndromes.clue: Conus lesions paralyze the pelvic floor and cause early sphincter dysfunction; cauda equina lesions give a flaccid, areflexic peripheral-type paraplegia.
keySyndromes.quote: conus medullaris lesions result in early sphincter compromise, late pain, and symmetrical sensory manifestations

boardTraps.text: A lateral medullary or lateral pontine lesion can, rarely, produce a contralateral leg or trunk sensory deficit that looks like a spinal level.
boardTraps.quote: a lateral medullary or lateral pontine lesion may, on rare occasions, also account for sensory deficits in the contralateral leg or trunk or both

boardTraps.text: Upper and mid-cervical lesions can cause false localizing findings such as thoracic sensory levels, paresthesias and hand clumsiness or atrophy.
boardTraps.quote: False localizing sensory and motor findings, including thoracic sensory levels, proprioceptive sensory loss, paresthesias, and hand clumsiness or atrophy

boardTraps.text: Acute cord lesions cause flaccid paralysis (spinal shock) before the spastic picture develops, so absent tone early does not exclude a cord lesion.
boardTraps.quote: With acute lesions, the paralysis is flaccid as a result of spinal cord hypoexcitability, also known as spinal shock.

boardTraps.text: A sensory level does not tell intramedullary from extramedullary: even Brown-Sequard syndrome, though more common extramedullary, can occur intramedullary.
boardTraps.quote: a sensory level is not a reliable clue to distinguish intramedullary from extramedullary lesions

boardTraps.text: The conus versus cauda equina contrast (sphincter, pain, symmetry) is a tendency, not a rule.
boardTraps.quote: this subtle distinction is exceedingly challenging and not always present

boardTraps.text: In ALS the thenar muscles waste more than the hypothenar muscles (split-hand pattern).
boardTraps.quote: There may be selective wasting of the thenar over the hypothenar muscles, also known as the split-hand pattern of ALS.
